outline.description: This chapter establishes the technical foundation of the patents in suit and the procedural history of the litigation, ensuring the student understands the specific problem the technology seeks to solve.
subtopics: Parties to the litigation: Finesse Wireless, AT&T, and Nokia
Technical concept: Intermodulation Products (IMPs) and Passive Intermodulation (PIM)
The purpose of PIM Cancellation (PIM-C) in radio technology
Overview of the '134 and '775 patents
Procedural posture: From jury verdict to the District Court's denial of JMOL and the subsequent appeal

outline.description: This chapter explains the legal standards the Federal Circuit uses to review the district court's decisions, which is critical for understanding how the court reached its final conclusion.
subtopics: Reviewing the denial of Judgment as a Matter of Law (JMOL) for noninfringement
The 'Substantial Evidence' standard for jury findings of infringement
The 'Reasonable Juror' test: When a verdict is legally unsustainable
Reviewing the denial of a new trial on damages (Abuse of Discretion)
The distinction between de novo review and substantial evidence review

outline.description: This chapter analyzes the court's reasoning regarding the '134 patent, focusing on the specific claim limitations and the failure of the plaintiff's expert testimony.
subtopics: Claim 1 limitation: Sampling a passband of received signals
The 'Modeled PIM Path' vs. 'Interference Generating Signals' distinction
The logical impossibility of sampling a signal before it is generated
Analysis of Dr. Wells' contradictory testimony regarding signal mapping
The impact of self-contradictory expert testimony on the 'substantial evidence' standard

outline.description: This chapter breaks down the court's analysis of the '775 patent, focusing on claim construction, prosecution history, and the specific mathematical operations required for infringement.
subtopics: Claim 1 limitation: Seven third-order multiplications
Claim construction: 'Three signals' as separately identifiable vs. unique
Prosecution history: Whether Finesse surrendered scope over products with only two unique input signals
The failure to map three distinct multiplications to the seven claimed multiplications
The insufficiency of relying on complex conjugate and modulus operations to satisfy claim limitations

outline.description: This final chapter summarizes the court's ultimate ruling and explains the legal consequences of the reversal.
subtopics: Reversal of the district court's denial of JMOL
The logic for vacating the $166 million damages award
Summary of the court's findings on substantial evidence
Final order: Reversed and Vacated
